title: FOREIGN KEY & Referential Integrity
description: Enforce relationships, configure ON DELETE CASCADE, RESTRICT, and SET NULL, and avoid unindexed foreign key table locks.

data.text: A **FOREIGN KEY** (FK) constraint ensures that values in a child column match existing values in a parent table's primary or unique key. This guarantees referential integrity at the database storage engine layer.

data.title: Critical DBA Warning
data.text: PostgreSQL does NOT automatically create an index on foreign key columns! When deleting a parent row, PostgreSQL must perform a sequential full table scan on the child table to verify referential integrity, acquiring heavy share locks and killing production performance. ALWAYS index your foreign keys!

data.title: Foreign Key Definition with Explicit Index
data.content: Configuring cascade rules and child index.

data.text: What the Constraint Guarantees — and What It Costs

A foreign key guarantees that the child value exists in the parent. To do that, PostgreSQL takes a `FOR KEY SHARE` lock on the parent row whenever a child row referencing it is inserted or updated, and checks the child table whenever a parent row is deleted or its key updated. That check is what makes the missing child index so harmful: without an index it is a sequential scan **inside a lock**.

data.title: All Four Referential Actions, Demonstrated
data.content: Pick the action deliberately; the default (`NO ACTION`) is not always what you want.
data.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id         BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
    parent_id   BIGINT REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
    note        TEXT
);

-- The five referential actions:
--   NO ACTION   (default) error at the end of the statement -> deferrable
--   RESTRICT              error immediately, cannot be deferred
--   CASCADE               delete/update the child rows too
--   SET NULL              null the child column (must be nullable)
--   SET DEFAULT           set the child column to its DEFAULT

-- Verify which actions are configured
SELECT con.conname,
       pg_get_constraintdef(con.oid) AS definition
FROM pg_constraint con
JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = con.conrelid
WHERE c.relname = 'orders' AND con.contype = 'f';

data.text: Indexing the Child Side, and Finding Missing Indexes

data.title: Audit Every Foreign Key That Lacks an Index
data.content: Run this on any inherited schema; it usually finds several.
data.code:
SELECT conrelid::regclass AS child_table,
       a.attname          AS fk_column,
       con.conname        AS constraint_name
FROM pg_constraint con
JOIN pg_attribute a
  ON a.attrelid = con.conrelid AND a.attnum = ANY (con.conkey)
WHERE con.contype = 'f'
  AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1
      FROM pg_index i
      WHERE i.indrelid = con.conrelid
        AND i.indkey::int2[] @> con.conkey::int2[]   -- index covers the FK columns
  );

data.title: Deferrable Constraints Inside a Transaction
data.content: Useful when you must insert child-before-parent in one migration.

data.title: Foreign Keys Are Not Free
data.text: Each `INSERT` into a child table performs a lookup on the parent, and each parent `DELETE` scans the child. Both are fast with indexes, but on high-throughput ingestion (millions of inserts per minute) teams sometimes drop or defer enforcement during bulk loads with `ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE TRIGGER ALL` — then re-enable and validate afterwards.

data.title: Add a Foreign Key to an Existing Table
steps: Create a child table with data that has no constraints.
Add the constraint with `ADD CONSTRAINT ... FOREIGN KEY ... NOT VALID;` (instant, no scan).
Create the index on the child column and confirm with `\d+ child`.
data.expectedOutcome: A constraint added without blocking writers for more than a moment.

items.question: Does PostgreSQL create an index for a foreign key automatically?
items.answer: No. The parent side needs a unique index (usually from the primary key), but the child side gets nothing. Without an index, every parent delete or key update scans the child table while holding a lock.

items.question: What is the difference between `RESTRICT` and `NO ACTION`?
items.answer: `NO ACTION` can be deferred to the end of the transaction and only fails if the violation still exists; `RESTRICT` fails immediately and cannot be deferred.

items.question: Should I use `ON DELETE CASCADE` everywhere?
items.answer: Only where the child has no independent existence. Cascading from a `customers` table to `invoices` can erase financial records; cascading from `orders` to `order_items` is usually correct.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: A foreign key enforces that a child value exists in the parent, taking a `FOR KEY SHARE` lock on the parent row.
PostgreSQL creates no index on the child column — an unindexed foreign key turns parent deletes into locked sequential scans.
Choose the referential action consciously: `RESTRICT` to protect, `CASCADE` for owned children, `SET NULL` for optional relations.
Add constraints to large tables with `NOT VALID` plus `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` to avoid long blocking scans.
data.takeaway: "Index your foreign keys" plus "choose ON DELETE deliberately" is the answer interviewers are listening for.
